Does the same emotion sound the same in 11 languages?

One crying clip in English, and the matching crying clips in ten other languages — plus anger and happiness for contrast. 594 clips, 11 languages, 7 language families, 59 acoustic measurements per clip.

594 clips 11 languages · 7 families 3 emotions × 18 clips per cell 33 interpretable features 11 published corpora

Yes — but only in relative terms, and much more for crying than for laughing. Two languages do not sound alike in absolute acoustics: which language a clip comes from explains about three times more variance than which emotion it carries. What is shared is the direction the voice moves from each language's own baseline. Standardise every feature inside its own language and sadness pushes the voice the same way everywhere.

A classifier that has never heard the test language still recognises the emotion 57.6% of the time (random forest 62.3%) against 33.3% chance and a 33.5% permutation null — about three quarters of the 74.4% that same-language training reaches.

What was measured

Eleven languages, one published emotional-speech corpus each: Bangla (SUBESCO), German (EmoDB), Greek (AESDD), English (RAVDESS), Persian (ShEMO), Japanese (JVNV), Polish (nEMO), Russian (RESD), Turkish (TurEV-DB), Urdu (URDU-Dataset), Mandarin (CASIA). Three emotions per language — sad as the anchor, with angry and happy as contrasts, because "similar" is only measurable against something dissimilar. Eighteen clips per cell, 16 kHz mono, silence-trimmed, amplitude left untouched.

Each language comes from a different corpus, so language and recording condition are entangled. Three defences are built in:

  • Within-language standardisation. Every feature is z-scored inside its own language first. It works: language identity is recoverable from the raw features with 81.8% accuracy (chance 9.1%) but only 1.5% afterwards.
  • Gain-invariance repeat. Dropping the features that would shift with a different recording level changes nothing: same-emotion r = +0.32 against -0.15, transfer 57.1%.
  • Permutation null. Emotion labels shuffled inside each language, 150 times, give 33.5%.

Finding 1 — crying has a common acoustic signature

Sadness: the features that move furthest, averaged over the 11 languages

Anger is the mirror image — the same two spectral-balance features at the top with the signs reversed, 11 of 11 languages agreeing. The universal part of emotional speech is mostly vocal effort: how hard the voice is driven, read off the balance between low- and high-frequency energy, with pitch level following along.

Finding 2 — happiness is the weak link

Not one feature survives correction for happiness (best q = 0.10). The classifier agrees:

true emotionrecognised in a foreign language most common confusion
sad 71.2%→ happy (19.7%)
angry 57.6%→ happy (30.3%)
happy 43.9% → angry (31.3%), sad (24.7%)

Happiness shares high vocal effort with anger and has no reliable signature of its own in this feature set. Whatever separates excited-positive from excited-negative is not in these 33 measurements — and may well be language-specific convention.

Transfer tracks how separable the emotions are inside that corpus to begin with (r = 0.66, p = 0.027). English and Russian transfer poorly because their corpora are internally hard, not because those languages are acoustically exotic.

Urdu is the real outlier: internally separable (0.74) yet transferring at chance (0.35). It is also the only corpus here that is not acted — the URDU-Dataset is harvested from talk shows. The biggest break in cross-lingual similarity in this experiment is spontaneous versus acted speech, not one language versus another.

Finding 4 — profiles transfer, single clips barely do

Across 160,380 cross-language clip pairs, two clips of the same emotion are closer than two clips of different emotions — mean distance 7.58 against 8.04, Cohen's d = 0.24 — but the overlap is large (AUC 0.57). A single foreign clip is only weakly attracted to its emotional neighbours; the regularity appears once clips are averaged into a profile. Expect cross-lingual emotion recognition on single short utterances to stay noisy even where the underlying code is genuinely shared.

The figures

Caveats

  • Ten of eleven corpora are acted emotion. Acted sadness is a performance of crying, not crying.
  • One corpus per language: "language" and "corpus" cannot be fully separated. The standardisation and the gain-invariance repeat bound the problem; they do not remove it.
  • Four corpora expose no speaker identity, so speaker variance is partly confounded with emotion in those cells.
  • Turkish clips are single words (median 0.66 s against 2.4 s elsewhere), which limits every contour and timing feature there.
  • 18 clips per cell is small — hence the confidence intervals, FDR correction and permutation null on every claim.
  • The emotion labels are the corpora's own; no listening test was run.
